analysis.one_liner: Makes an executive order law requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and banning barcode ballot scanners.
analysis.headline: The bill has four Republican cosponsors and no committee or floor action since it was referred to three House committees in March 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would make Executive Order 14248, signed by President Trump in March 2025, permanent law. The order requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship — such as a passport or a REAL ID that shows citizenship — on the national mail voter registration form, bans voting machines that count ballots by barcode, and directs the Justice Department to take action against states that count mail ballots sent by Election Day rather than received by Election Day. Because it would be a statute rather than an executive order, it could not be simply reversed by a future president.
analysis.who_benefits: Supporters who want proof-of-citizenship rules locked in get a durable rule: an executive order can be revoked by the next administration, but a statute cannot be without another act of Congress. Incumbent officeholders also gain from an electorate narrowed by new registration requirements, since voters who lack citizenship documents are removed from the pool.

how_it_helps.text: Codifying the order gives it the force of statute, so the rules could not be reversed by a later president the way an executive order can.

The national mail voter registration form would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship, with acceptable documents including a passport or a REAL ID-compliant identification that indicates citizenship.

The Election Assistance Commission would be directed to prohibit voting systems that use a barcode or QR code in the vote-counting process and to recertify or decertify existing equipment under the new standards.

The Justice Department would be directed to enforce federal election law against states that do not require mail ballots to be received, rather than merely sent, by Election Day in order to be counted.

analysis.who_pays: Eligible voters who do not have citizenship documents on hand bear the cost: a passport costs money and takes weeks to obtain, and the acceptable documents can fail to match a voter's current legal name after marriage. State and local election offices would face new federal mandates and possible Justice Department enforcement, and voting equipment vendors would lose certification for barcode-counting machines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters without passports and state election offices

drawbacks.text: Every federal voter registration would require documentary proof of citizenship, limited to documents such as a passport or a REAL ID that indicates citizenship; millions of eligible voters do not have a passport, and birth certificates that do not match a current legal name would not qualify.
The Justice Department would be directed to sue states over their mail-ballot receipt deadlines, adding federal enforcement against state election practices.
Rescinding all previous certifications of voting equipment based on prior standards could force states to replace machines they already use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a uniform, durable rule aimed at preventing noncitizen voting, which research has found to be extremely rare in practice. The cost is that the same requirement screens out eligible citizens — disproportionately lower-income voters who lack passports and voters whose legal names have changed — and imposes new burdens and litigation risk on states. For most readers, the barriers to eligible voters are the larger effect; the bill writes the rule into permanent law without those trade-offs being tested in a committee hearing or a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, and with only a handful of cosponsors none of them has taken it up.

narrative.text: Representative Abraham Hamadeh of Arizona, joined by Representative Claudia Tenney, introduced the bill on March 31, 2025.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means committees for the portions within each committee's jurisdiction.
Four Republicans have cosponsored the bill; no further action has been taken since the referral, and the Congress is still in session.
The bill codifies Executive Order 14248, which President Trump signed on March 25, 2025; the Congressional Research Service describes that order as restricting voting in federal elections.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nothing has happened to change anyone's position, but eligible voters who would face new registration hurdles are better off while the bill sits untouched in committee; no industry or group has gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voters spared new registration hurdles, for now

for.name: Rep. Abraham Hamadeh
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify Executive Order 14248 as permanent law.

for.name: Rep. Claudia Tenney
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: President Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Signed Executive Order 14248, the election rules this bill would write into law.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Republican; no Democrat has joined, and no vote has been held that would show the full chamber's split.

industries.note: The underlying order bans systems that count ballots using barcodes or QR codes and rescinds certifications granted under earlier standards, which could force states to retire and replace machines. Some election officials say barcode-counting systems are tested and reliable, so the loss is a contested policy question rather than a clear public gain or loss.

Election offices would face new federal mandates on registration, database access, and mail-ballot deadlines, plus the risk of Justice Department enforcement. Some of that friction serves the federal rules' stated goal; some of it falls on routine election administration.

A registration rule that screens out voters without citizenship documents shrinks the electorate, and the voters screened out are disproportionately lower-income. Incumbents who run under the narrowed electorate gain insulation from it.

analysis.trajectory: With only four cosponsors and no action from any of the three committees months after referral, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or markup this Congress unless House leadership elevates it. Most bills referred to multiple committees with sparse support die at this stage, while the underlying executive order remains in effect and is being tested in litigation on its own.
